## What this does

NASA's Black Marble satellite data shows how bright places are at night. Brighter usually means more people, buildings, and electricity. In this notebook I used the `blackmarbler` package to pull nighttime lights for Hawaiʻi at three time scales (daily, monthly, and yearly), made a map, and looked at how brightness changed from 2012 to 2022.

## Setup

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(blackmarbler)
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyterra)
library(lubridate)
library(tigris)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tibble)
library(exactextractr)

options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
```

NASA Earthdata login, needed to download Black Marble data. (I'm using the class login here so my own password isn't posted on GitHub.)

```{r bearer-token}
bearer <- get_nasa_token(username = "connorflynn",
                         password = "EarthData120")
```

## Region of interest

The region has to be an `sf` polygon in WGS84 (EPSG:4326). I used Hawaiʻi's counties and cropped out the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands so the maps focus on the main islands.

```{r roi}
roi_hawaii <- counties(state = "HI", cb = TRUE, year = 2022) |>
  st_transform(4326) |>
  st_crop(xmin = -160.5, xmax = -154.5, ymin = 18.5, ymax = 22.5) |>
  filter(NAME != "Kalawao")
```

## Three time scales

Black Marble comes in three versions:

- **VNP46A2:** daily (one night)
- **VNP46A3:** monthly (average of a month)
- **VNP46A4:** yearly (average of a year)

```{r daily}
# Daily: February 5, 2021
r_20210205 <- bm_raster(roi_sf = roi_hawaii,
                        product_id = "VNP46A2",
                        date = "2021-02-05",
                        bearer = bearer)
```

```{r monthly}
# Monthly: October 2021 (the day is ignored)
r_202110 <- bm_raster(roi_sf = roi_hawaii,
                      product_id = "VNP46A3",
                      date = "2021-10-01",
                      bearer = bearer)
```

```{r yearly}
# Yearly: 2021
r_2021 <- bm_raster(roi_sf = roi_hawaii,
                    product_id = "VNP46A4",
                    date = 2021,
                    bearer = bearer)
```

## Map: October 2021

Most places are dark and a few are very bright, so I used a log scale. That way both dim towns and bright cities show up on the map.

```{r map-oct-2021}
r <- r_202110 |> terra::mask(roi_hawaii)

r <- log(r + 1)

ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r) +
  geom_sf(data = roi_hawaii, fill = NA, color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "black",
                       mid = "yellow",
                       high = "red",
                       midpoint = 4.5,
                       na.value = "transparent") +
  labs(title = "Hawaiʻi Nighttime Lights: October 2021") +
  coord_sf() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
        legend.position = "none")
```

Honolulu on Oʻahu is by far the brightest spot. Smaller bright spots show up around Kahului (Maui), Hilo and Kona (Big Island), and Līhuʻe (Kauaʻi).

## Trend: 2012 to 2022

This pulls the yearly average brightness for each county from 2012 to 2022.

```{r annual-trend}
# Download each year's map, then average the brightness inside each county
ntl_df <- map_dfr(2012:2022, function(y) {
  r_y <- bm_raster(roi_sf = roi_hawaii,
                   product_id = "VNP46A4",
                   date = y,
                   bearer = bearer)
  tibble(NAME = roi_hawaii$NAME,
         date = y,
         ntl_mean = exact_extract(r_y, roi_hawaii, fun = "mean"))
})

ntl_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = ntl_mean)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") +
  facet_wrap(~NAME, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = "Average nighttime brightness",
       title = "Hawaiʻi Counties: Yearly Average Nighttime Lights, 2012–2022") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2012, 2022, 4)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

**What I see:** Honolulu County is much brighter than the other counties every year. Each panel has its own y-axis, so look at the shape of the bars to see whether a county got brighter or darker over time: \_\_\_.

## Daily data: January 2023

This pulls each night of **January 2023** and averages the brightness in each county. I only used one month, because pulling every day up to today would take a very long time. If a night fails to download (for example, because of clouds), it gets skipped.

```{r daily-extract}
#| warning: false

jan_2023 <- seq.Date(from = ymd("2023-01-01"), to = ymd("2023-01-31"), by = 1)

ntl_daily <- map_dfr(jan_2023, function(d) {
  tryCatch({
    r_d <- bm_raster(roi_sf = roi_hawaii,
                     product_id = "VNP46A2",
                     date = d,
                     bearer = bearer)
    tibble(NAME = roi_hawaii$NAME,
           date = d,
           ntl_mean = exact_extract(r_d, roi_hawaii, fun = "mean"))
  }, error = function(e) NULL)
})
```

```{r daily-plot}
ggplot(ntl_daily, aes(x = date, y = ntl_mean, color = NAME)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Daily Nighttime Brightness by County, January 2023",
       x = NULL, y = "Average nighttime brightness", color = "County") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Daily data jumps around a lot from night to night, mostly because of clouds and the moon. That's why monthly or yearly averages are better for seeing long-term trends, and why daily data is useful for one-time events like power outages.
